answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote lists this line under Wooden’s memoir They Call Me Coach (1972). Its transcription carries a comma the circulated version drops — “The main ingredient of stardom, is the rest of the team” — and we could not read the book to settle which is the book’s own punctuation.

source.heading: Credited to the 1972 memoir

source.excerpt: The main ingredient of stardom is the rest of the team.
trail: Wikiquote’s John Wooden page ↗ lists the line in its section for They Call Me Coach (1972), transcribed as “The main ingredient of stardom, is the rest of the team.”
Wikipedia’s bibliography ↗ confirms the book: They Call Me Coach, John Wooden with Jack Tobin, 1972, Word Books.
The Internet Archive’s 1972 scan ↗ is lending-restricted, so neither its text nor its search index could be used to check the comma or the page.
Quote Investigator ↗ has not traced this saying, so Wikiquote’s attribution stands unchallenged and unrefined.
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote transcribes the line with a comma after “stardom”. That comma is not grammatical and may be an artefact of transcription rather than the book’s own punctuation — but since we could not read the book, we are flagging the difference rather than deciding it.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of John Wooden and his publishers
source.rightsNote: They Call Me Coach was first published in 1972, well after the 1930 cutoff for United States public domain, so the text is in copyright. Rights sit with Wooden’s estate and the book’s publishers.

author.name: John Wooden
author.heading: About John Wooden
author.bio: John Robert Wooden won ten NCAA championships in twelve years at UCLA, including seven in a row, and was the first person inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame as both a player and a coach. He is remembered less for the trophies than for the teaching — short, plain maxims delivered to teenagers, and the “Pyramid of Success” he built around the idea that success is something you measure against yourself.

context.heading: The coach who distrusted stars
lead: Wooden won ten NCAA titles with some of the most famous players in the sport, and spent much of his career arguing that the fame was a by-product rather than the engine. This line is that argument compressed to one sentence.
It is also a recruiting pitch in disguise: it tells the star what he needs, and tells everyone else they are it.
